transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya, Ethan, Jing, Liam (Stratagem Health)

Summary:
Brief technical deep dive to finalize multi-region failover policy, verify KV cache warmstart behavior for on-prem/private deployments, and agree on runbook steps for a potential emergency evacuation to Redwood Dedicated in a region outage. Customer emphasized strict egress controls and HSM-based KMS, wants low-risk playbook.

Topics:
- Routing policy options: weighted routing, sticky sessions, session affinity, circuit breakers
- Regional capacity and scaling: reserved vs burstable, cost implications
- KV cache warmstart/priming strategies across regions and on-prem connectors
- Batching and quantization fallbacks for graceful degradation
- DNS TTL, traffic shift playbook, and operator steps for canary + full cutover

Links shared: Deck: https://redwood.app/drive/stratagem-health/regional-evac-playbook-v1.pdf
Benchmark sheet: https://sheets.redwood/regional-benchmarks-2026 (note: internal link)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick agenda — we want to go through the policy options for routing, KV warmstart behavior, and then step through an evacuation runbook for on prem to dedicated failover. is that still where you want to spend most of the hour?
[00:16] Priya: yes, that's perfect. we had a couple internal ops nightmares recently, so we want the playbook to be as prescriptive as possible. especially around K M S keys in H S M — that is non negotiable.
[00:29] Diego: noted. i'll focus on the runtime implications — latency/throughput and kv warmstart times. maya will cover the operator runbook and dns/route suggestions.
[00:38] Ethan: quick bit of context — our on-prem setup is air gapped for PHI sync, outbound is tightly controlled, we use an HSM cluster for KMS, and current traffic spikes are ~6k rps peak per region with burst to 12k.
[00:54] Maya: thanks. so two constraints i'm hearing: limited egress and strict KMS/HSM. we should talk about private deployment connectors and whether redwood Private can live in your VPC or we need an on-prem agent.
[01:10] Jing: yes, we can't have raw token material leave HSM. any fallback model or routing option must continue to honor key residency.
[01:20] Diego: right — for on prem we typically integrate with customer's KMS via our connector, or we can do a bring-your-own-key approach where the signing happens inside your HSM and only cert artifacts are exchanged. the runtime doesn't need raw keys to serve; it needs encrypted model keys and a sealed decrypt step at load. the subtle part is when we do a cross-region failover, reloading caches triggers decrypt+load operations which require KMS roundtrips.
[01:45] Priya: so what are warmstart numbers? if we failover to eu-west from us-west, how long to have KV cache hot so p95 doesn't spike to garbage?
[01:56] Diego: good question — depends on model seq length and cache footprint. in our internal benchmarks with a 350B-ish model, a cold start for KV cache priming can add 20–45s of tail latency for the first few requests if you don't pre-warm. with prefix caching and targeted rehydration we can bring most hot prefixes online in 6–12s for typical conversational workloads. but full KV warm (all sessions) is minutes.
[02:22] Ethan: 6–12 seconds for the first user is ok, but we have low tolerance for broad customer-visible spikes. what's the approach for gradual rehydration?
[02:34] Diego: two levers: 1) proactive rewarm — stream top N prefixes from the source region into the fallback region ahead of cutover; 2) on-demand lazy fill with a prioritized queue so requests see progressive quality improvements. proactive rewarm requires network transfer of small KV blobs; for on-prem, that hits your egress rules, so we can stage via an s3/bucket in your control plane or use an AWS PrivateLink.
[02:59] Liam: for on-prem to cloud, we can't open arbitrary outbound. any transfer needs a dedicated egress policy and approval window.
[03:07] Maya: which is why the runbook defines an 'egress approval' step — we call ops to open a conftunnel for X minutes and then pre-warm keys. we'll include exact IP ranges and fingerprints.
[03:19] Priya: i want to see the playbook language for that step.
[03:23] Maya: noted, will include.
[03:26] Diego: on the runtime side, batching behavior affects warmstart — continuous batching means we can saturate GPU throughput, but it also means the first N requests may be batched with a warm-priming request and see increased latency variance. we can tweak batch windows and target latency SLOs. in Dedicated you get finer-grained controls: max batch latency, queue depth per worker.
[03:51] Ethan: so if we tighten batch windows to reduce p95, cost goes up?
[03:56] Diego: yes, tighter windows => smaller batches => lower throughput efficiency => higher cost per token. but you can pair that with quantization to offset cost. which leads into model fallback discussion.
[04:06] Priya: we definitely want graceful degradation. what does a quantization fallback look like operationally?
[04:12] Diego: typical pattern: normal ops on full precision (fp16 or int8/channel-wise tuned). on capacity strain or during failover, we can route to a quantized variant (4-bit or 8-bit) which reduces GPU memory and increases throughput but may shift some outputs slightly. we recommend a two-tier fallback: first fall back to int8-tuned variant, if still overloaded, switch some traffic to 4-bit variant but only on non-critical routes.
[04:38] Priya: are those models always kept loaded? the concern is memory and load time.
[04:44] Diego: good call — we keep the primary loaded. fallback quantized variants can be kept in a standby pool (warm but not fully resident) or kept as quick warm images that load in 8–22s depending on the model and quantization format. tradeoff is memory vs load time. for DR, we recommend pre-loading the int8 fallback on a smaller standby pool in the fallback region so you can immediately shift traffic without a heavy load penalty.
[05:06] Maya: note that standby pools consume reserved capacity, so cost implications. i'll capture those numbers in the pricing follow-up.
[05:13] Ethan: how about network routing — weighted dns vs active-active with sticky sessions? our application ties some user sessions to cache entries so affinity matters.
[05:22] Diego: two main architectures: active-active with sticky sessions (client or proxy level sticky) or active-passive with fast failover. active-active gives better utilization but you need strong cache coherency or prefix replication. sticky sessions help, but if you evicted the KV in region B, requests routed there will see quality drop. active-passive with automated promotion reduces cross-region consistency issues but needs capacity reserved in the passive region.
[05:47] Priya: capacity is the big budget item — can we do a hybrid where we reserve a small pool in passive region and allow burst to other clouds only if cost center approves?
[05:57] Maya: yes, Redwood Dedicated supports burst policies and cost triggers; we'll include an ASA for threshold alarms that auto-notify your ops and optionally open a short-term burst window.
[06:06] Jing: from a security perspective, we need audit logs for cross-region transfers and explicit consent records for KMS use. do you capture those?
[06:14] Diego: yes — audit trail for model loads, KMS calls, and cache priming transfers are captured per-request. logs can be exported to your SIEM. we also support per-tenant RBAC so only approved operators can trigger the playbook.
[06:27] Liam: what's the recommended DNS TTL during a failover? we saw slow switches previously because our TTLs were 300s.
[06:33] Maya: recommend lowering to 30s in the canary window. runbook step: pre-cutover reduce TTL to 30s 10 minutes before canary, run canary for 5 min, then full shift. after stabilization, increase TTL back to 300s. we'll document exact times.
[06:48] Ethan: what about connection draining? we need in-flight requests to finish rather than drop.
[06:52] Diego: Redwood runtime supports graceful drain at worker level — you can set a drain timeout (default 120s). during canary we recommend 60–120s depending on your average request duration.
[07:02] Priya: earlier you mentioned prefix replication — does that replicate entire KV or just hot keys?
[07:09] Diego: usually hot keys only; we compute an LRU heatmap and replicate top N prefixes. full replication is expensive. hot-key replication can be incremental and prioritized by recent activity.
[07:20] Ethan: will the replication trigger KMS decrypt on the other side?
[07:24] Diego: yes, each load will attempt KMS unwrap. that's why we need a KMS path open or a cross-region key policy. for strict HSM-only setups, we propose a 2-step: export encrypted key blob via approved channel and have the receiving region perform unwrap via a wrapped key exchange with your HSM. it's secure but has setup overhead.
[07:47] Jing: that setup will require our security team's signoff. can you include config snippets?
[07:50] Maya: yes, we'll add sample CLI commands and firewall/ip details in the doc.
[07:56] [00:08:00] Speaker 1 (muffled): um, quick q — how do we prevent double-pay or race conditions when promoting a region?
[08:07] Diego: good point — our rollout uses a single control-plane transaction and feature flags. we mark the source region as draining, flip weight to 0, and then promote primary model variant in the target. we also provide idempotency tokens in the client SDK to avoid duplicate requests.
[08:22] Priya: timeline wise, if we start the runbook, how long until we consider the target region fully primary?
[08:28] Maya: end-to-end with pre-approved egress and pre-warm of hot prefixes — can be 2–6 minutes for targeted cutover. without pre-warm, expect quality convergence over 5–15 minutes.
[08:39] Ethan: ok. let's run that benchmark.
[08:42] Diego: i'll run a benchmark simulating canary then full shift. i'll include p50/p95/p99, token cost delta, and KV cache hit ratio during the cutover.
[08:51] Priya: please add a scenario where the target region has lower-capacity GPU families (e.g., a quantized-only pool). we might route only non-PHI or lower-sensitivity traffic there.
[09:02] Diego: yes — policy routing can map by tag: sensitive=true -> route to region A only; sensitive=false -> fallback pool. rules can be as fine-grained as request tag, API key, or route.
[09:14] Maya: quick interruption — the runbook also needs clear operator cues: who gets paged at each threshold, what to do if KMS unwrap fails, when to rollback. we'll codify checkpoint gates.
[09:26] Jing: what if HSM is unreachable? do you have an offline key sharing option?
[09:31] Diego: we can support a sealed key exchange: you generate a wrapped key blob that can be staged in object storage and later unwrapped by your HSM under emergency conditions. that requires pre-provisioning and strict change controls.
[09:45] Priya: that sounds acceptable with proper controls.
[09:48] Maya: i'll add templated change control language for signoff.
[09:51] [00:10:00] Ethan: another ops question — during surge, how do you prioritize business-critical routes?
[10:00] Diego: Redwood supports per-route priority levels and weighted routing. you can set a hard SLO for critical routes and configure admission control to reject or queue low-priority traffic. there's also model-based throttling where you degrade non-critical routes to a smaller quantized model automatically.
[10:17] Priya: and we get metrics for how much traffic was degraded?
[10:20] Diego: yes — Console shows token counts, degraded requests, and quality deltas per route.
[10:25] Liam: can that be exported to our PagerDuty / OpsPost?
[10:29] Maya: yes — we have webhooks and integrations.
[10:32] [00:12:30] Diego: quick detail on KV eviction: eviction is LRU within a tenant's shard. we also provide cold TTLs and an optional pinned prefix set for VIP sessions. pinned prefixes are not evicted until explicitly removed. good for key accounts.
[10:46] Priya: pinning is important for one of our partners. fine.
[10:49] Ethan: what about background rewarm bandwidth — how much network do we need for top N prefixes?
[10:54] Diego: depends on prefix size. for our typical chat workloads, top 100k prefixes might be ~200–500MB compressed. we can incrementalize so you never transfer huge blobs in one shot.
[11:06] Priya: that's doable if we schedule during maintenance window.
[11:10] Diego: also note that for quantized fallback, model size shrinks dramatically — e.g., 8-bit variant might be ~40% smaller and 4-bit ~20% of original; load times improve accordingly.
[11:22] [00:15:00] Maya: let's step through the runbook play-by-play: pre-checks, egress approval, pre-warm, canary cut, monitor p95/p99 and hit ratio, escalate or full cut, then post-cut stabilization and increase TTL.
[11:36] Priya: can you show sample thresholds?
[11:39] Maya: recommended canary: 1% traffic for 5min, target p95 not worse than 1.5x baseline and hit ratio > 70% for hot prefixes. if either fails, rollback. for full cut, ensure capacity is at least 1.2x expected baseline with standby pools active.
[11:58] Ethan: ok, 1.2x reserve is acceptable.
[12:02] Diego: a note on observability — include token-level tracing and per-prefix counters, not just overall latency, because p95 can hide hot prefix storms.
[12:12] Jing: regarding compliance, we need retention and redaction rules for transcripts and logs. can logs be filtered for PHI?
[12:18] Diego: yes — we can configure scrubbing rules and only emit non-PII metrics to Redwood Console; full logs can go to your SIEM under your retention policy.
[12:27] [00:20:00] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) sorry, quick— do you have a sample terraform or helm snippet for on-prem agent?
[12:34] Maya: yes, we'll attach terraform snippets and an ops-runbook repo link.
[12:36] Link note: repo: https://git.redwood/internal/ops/playbooks/stratagem-evac
[12:41] Priya: great. i'd like the SSH fingerprints for your pre-warm host and the exact CIDR ranges.
[12:46] Maya: we'll include them in the secure doc and share via SSO-protected link.
[12:50] Diego: one more runtime optimization: KV sharding by tenant reduces cross-tenant noise and reduces replication scope. plus we can colocate hot-tenant shards in the same worker to reduce latency.
[13:03] Ethan: how do you handle sticky sessions when client IPs change because of mobile users?
[13:08] Diego: use token-based affinity — assign an affinity cookie or session token, not client IP. SDKs support that.
[13:15] Priya: last technical nit: during failover we must ensure audit trail shows who triggered the runbook. can that be correlatable to our internal ticket id?
[13:22] Maya: yes — runbook triggers accept an external correlation id and it's logged in every step.
[13:26] [00:30:00] -- quick 5 minute demo skipped here (we referenced a slide and Diego's laptop share) --
[18:26] Diego: demo takeaway — i showed a simulated canary shift; p95 rose from 120ms to 170ms during the first 30s then normalized to 130ms after hot-prefix rehydration. the sheet has step timestamps.
[18:39] Priya: that's within our loose SLO. can we see the raw trace for the canary?
[18:43] Diego: yes — i'll attach the trace links.
[18:46] Maya: okay, wrapping to next steps.
[18:50] Priya: recapping from our side — we'll validate the egress change window and share KMS HSM contact.
[18:56] Ethan: we'll also try to identify 2–3 VIP prefixes to pin.
[19:01] Jing: security will review the sealed-key exchange language.
[19:05] Maya: Redwood will deliver the DR playbook draft, the terraform snippets, the benchmark plan, and the pricing delta for standby pools + burst.
[19:13] Diego: action items i have: run 2-region benchmark, attach CSV and graph to the spreadsheet, include delta for quantized fallbacks.
[19:21] Priya: timeline ok?
[19:23] Maya: yes — we'll do initial draft by Friday (2026-06-12) and benchmark by Tuesday (2026-06-16).
[19:29] Liam: any blockers?
[19:31] Priya: firewall approval and security signoff; otherwise none.
[19:35] Maya: great — thanks everyone. i'll send the notes and links.
[19:39] [00:56:00] End

Meeting recap (short):
- Agreed on hybrid active-active/active-passive approach with pinned prefixes for VIPs and standby pools preloaded with int8 fallback.
- Runbook will include egress approval step, DNS TTL manipulation, canary thresholds (1% for 5min), and rollback gates.
- Action items and next steps captured above; customer to share on-prem topology + HSM/KMS contact.
